utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Gerard Dobbyn, our Case Manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, and today, one of our interns, Andrew Pattel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery for the Stanisic Defence. And we shall have Mr. Zecevic joining us very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue his examination-in-chief, I remind of the solemn declaration you made yesterday. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, yesterday we finished the questioning at the time when I asked for us to adjourn sooner because I noticed that you were having problems. So if at any point you feel that you might develop -- be developing a headache or you feel fatigue, I will ask for a break to be given to you so that you can concentrate on your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, yesterday, when you were looking at the document on the screen, you spoke about the speeches given by Mr. Kadiric and Talundzic in which they proposed the forming of the Prijedor CSB. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting with Mr. Zupljanin, were Mr. Talundzic and Kadiric involved in any activities with the aim of continuing this process? Was there any debate about this debate -- about this subject?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was a short period, if we're talking about the 9th of April, when Mr. Zupljanin came, and the meeting where the dispatch arrived was the 29th of April, so within the span of those 20 days, there were obviously some processes going on but it was not very easy to notice that. The one thing that I observed is something that happened in the second ten days, from the 20th onwards, and what I noticed was that whenever I went to Chief Talundzic, Avdo Hebib would come as well. I already said that. He was an assistant minister. And no assistant minister used to come as often as he did. There were also some things that, superficially, if you're not paying attention enough, seemed insignificant but were rather out of the ordinary. What I'm talking about. I'm talking about a frequent occurrence in which there -- wealthy entrepreneurs would be coming to the SUP building to see Chief Hasan, but that was not something ordinary. For example, I saw a man who was called Cuko. He would come in his jeep right in front of the stairs and the entrance to the SUP, which is only allowed to be done by official and police cars. However, he didn't take any care whatsoever, so he parked his vehicle wherever he wanted. So all this plethora of minute details speaks something about the situation which was not quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, just one question more. Avdo Hebib, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by his surname, he was a Muslim. But, then again, I'm telling you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And those people that you described coming to the SUP building in Prijedor and particularly Cuko --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuko was a Muslim too. I forgot his surname, but I know where his restaurant was, and I know that he was quite a prominent figure in the catering business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these people whom you described coming to see Chief Talundzic to the SUP, what was their ethnicity, including Cuko, and the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep talking about specific examples but maybe I should rather paint the whole situation to you. My job required me to go see the chief at least three times a day to ask him something or seek approval. So whenever I went to see him, there would be someone coming into his office, and saying "Merhaba, Hasan" and he would reply, "Merhaba." We used to say good morning or good afternoon. That was never the way that we greeted each other before. Later on I would say the same to Hasan. I would say "Merhaba." And then when he came to my office he says, "God help you, hero," which is a Serbian phrase. And I didn't know what to respond. So he asked me, "So why are you using the Muslim greeting if you don't know your own?" So that was just an illustration of the whole situation. All these greeting phrases had never been used before because we were an institution that was serving, that was at the disposal of all the citizens, and we should have stuck to the normal greeting in our tongue, which is good morning or good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the meeting of the 29th April 1992. Can you tell us briefly what preceded the meeting, when did you find out about the meeting, and how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the one on the 29th of April, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Briefly. This whole period in 1992 was divided into stages. The first stage was up to the multi-party elections. Second stage was between the multi-party elections and the 29th of April. And that's the one I'm going to talk about, although I told you everything about it already. And then we have a third stage, which occurred after the meeting of the 29th of April, and it lasted until the 30th of May, when an attack on Prijedor took place. So I'm talking about this third phase, in fact. Whatever I've been telling you this morning, and if you look at the whole picture, one could see that tensions were rising. And whoever was there on the spot and was able to listen to things, it was very easy to establish a connection between the meeting on the 9th, when Mr. Zupljanin was there, and when Fikret spoke about reorganisation and the separation and the creation of a new centre in Prijedor, and as a result of all of this, we are having this meeting of the 29th of April. I hadn't had any previous knowledge about this meeting being planned because I was somewhere out in the field doing my job relating to communications system. And when I came back, at around 1400 hours, all authorised officials including communications officers, which means the entire active and reserve police force, were invited, including the criminal investigation police, to assemble in a hall for a meeting. And that's all that was said. Now, I called my fellow communications officer. We went down. We just left one officer on duty because the -- one must never leave the centre -- communications centre unattended. So the meeting started, and I saw that the chair of the meeting was actually composed of five persons. They were sitting at a table, or maybe two tables, from left to right. The first one was Mirza Mujagic, who was at the time the president of the SDA. So from left to right. Next to him was sitting Cehajic. I don't know what his first name was. Either Muhamed or Muharem. Anyway, it begins with an M. He was the president of the municipality. In the middle was sitting the chairperson, so to say, Hasan Talundzic, the chief of the police station. And next to him, Fikret Kadiric was sitting, an associate of his, and I think that, at the time, he was the commander of the traffic police. And the fifth one viewing from left to right was Simo Miskovic. He wasn't working at the police at the time. He was a retired police officer, but as far as I know, at that point, he was the president of the SDS. I cannot be positive about that. I think that he was the president of the SDS, but I wasn't a member. I think he was the president. So let me continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just tell me, where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The venue was the hall that was within our station. It was not in the main building, actually, but across the yard there was this hall and there was some garages. And this hall was normally used for the meetings of police employees. However, this hall, on this occasion, was too small to accommodate all the people who gathered there. I don't know how many of them, but it was packed. People were even standing outside in front of the door. There are some pillars, just like in this room, and I was standing and leaning on one of those pillars, about 5 metres from the chair. The meeting eventually started, and there was only one item on the agenda. The chairs addressed those in attendance and raised various reasons, based on which we, that is to say, the Prijedor police station, should cease to belong to the Banja Luka centre and join the Sarajevo centre. At that point, we were already owed two salaries, and these two salaries that were in arrears were presented by them as the main reason. They said that we would be paid one of these salaries on the following day, and the next, several days later. All the explanations they provided went along that line, and all those present seemed to be happy with them. They were maybe only two or three of them who raised their voice and I think they were Serbs. I knew Milivoje Mutic, for instance, one of them, whereas the others I didn't know them because they were on the reserve force. They spoke against the proposal; the rest were silent. Or those who did take the floor said that they were in agreement with what was stated because we would refuse to go on working without being paid. The meeting lasted perhaps 45 minutes, an hour, I'm not sure. At any rate, everything was over quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Did Mr. Miskovic speak at the meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was present there, but he didn't speak. He may have said something, very little, and of such insignificance that I didn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was it who set out this proposal that the Prijedor police station should be connected directly to the Sarajevo centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the chief of the station, Hasan Talundzic, who was the chair, and seated in the middle of the room. But, likewise, Mr. Talundzic and the president of -- Mr. -- the president of the municipality, him -- also took the floor and others who provided explanations. Now, who said what at that point, I really don't remember. Anyway, the general idea that was expressed at the meeting was what I just related to you. Only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Jankovic. Did anything happen during the meeting which --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At that point, the entire police station was empty. There was only a duty policeman at the front door, and there was only the duty communications officer in the communications centre, the one that I was superior to. And at one point, the communications officer sent word to me through the duty officer at the front door that I should show up there because they were having some problems with communication devices, because we didn't have a phone in the conference room so he wasn't able to call me there. So I went up there. He told me it was urgent. I left the meeting, which went on. There was Dusko Sarac there. He was the communications duty officer. He showed me a dispatch that he had received from Sarajevo. It had been coded. The dispatch bore an address and it required him to send it on to the municipalities that were linked with us, i.e., Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica. However, he was unable to, because the Banja Luka communications officer refused to connect him to the various stations that he needed. So he applied to me, asking what was -- what he was supposed to do. In general, whenever communications officers had problems with a dispatch, they consulted me for a decision rather than inadvertently make an erroneous move. I would then cast a glance at the dispatch to gauge its importance and decide on my next steps. At times, a dispatch can wait; at others, it can't. Normally such dispatches would have their designation of urgency at the top. This one read: Very urgent. In our police standard procedure, this was the top of the scale of urgency and it had normally only to do with matters of state significance. As a rule, such dispatches had to be sent to the head office of an organisational unit, i.e., the chief of the station, as a matter of utmost urgency. If he wasn't there, then the dispatch would have to be sent to his deputy with the deputy being obliged to find the chief as soon as may be, in order to convey to him the contents of the dispatch. And, as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, were you able to read the contents of the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, even before, whatever the contents of the dispatch, where I saw that it was impossible to apply the standard procedure, I would decide on what measures are to be taken on the basis of the contents of the dispatch. So I cast a cursory glance at this dispatch and saw that it had been issued by the minister, pursuant to the decision of the Presidency. Well, I can't really list all the various items one, two, three, but I could tell that it had to do with the mobilisation of the police and Territorial Defence, that it had to do with the need to cordon off all the strategic roads, vital institutions, barracks, with the need to disarm the army in the barracks, and it said that wherever opposition was met, one should engage in combat. To my mind, it was a shock. I had been working for the police force for quite a long time by then, and I had occasion to see a variety of contents but none of them produced such a shock as this one. My understanding of it was that it marked the beginning of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A moment, please. Can I show you a document at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 1D00150. In the Zupljanin Defence binder, it's behind tab 9. Can I have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to apologise and kindly ask you something. I made a mistake of leaving my jacket in that room outside the door here where my reading glasses are, and I think the lady saw me leave the jacket. If she could go and get it, or I should perhaps, because I don't have prescription on these glasses. I left my jacket on the door, and it's got my reading glasses in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jankovic, we'll wait for you to get your glasses then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While this document is coming up, Your Honour, I need to bring to your attention something that I raised before. The English translation of this document has something in the upper right-hand corner that was a handwritten notation which does not appear on the B/C/S version of this document that's in e-court. I brought this to the attention of the Defence previously, and I believe we marked it as an additional number. I believe we marked this as 150.1. So for that to be consistent, I think we should bring that version up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think in the English version, we would be better off with - what is it again? - 1D150.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This dispatch isn't it accurate. It isn't the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Behind 9.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it doesn't say "very urgent," whereas the original did. In the upper right-hand corner, we don't have that designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should show the third document in the binder in e-court. That's the document referred to by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see it now? It does say "very urgent" up there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a poor copy, admittedly, but it does look like the original. It does have the heading, although can you barely make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, is this the dispatch that you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What, with all the blurs and blots, I would say that it is. No, actually. Is this the one? No, please, find it somewhere. I did see it. You had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I'm sorry, let me explain. There are various copies of the document. I showed you a copy which has already been admitted into evidence, and this is another copy, different from the one you saw, but it does contain all the elements you refer to like "very urgent"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of any copies. I only know of the document that I had in my hands, and I can tell that it says "very urgent" here. And it is not insignificant, let me tell you. Under our rules governing communication, dispatches are classified according to the varying degrees of urgency. O stands for regular; that's the lowest on the scale. Then you have D. Next on the scale, DD. Still next, DX. It only reads X here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you look at the top, at the heading? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the topmost is "very urgent."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that it reads "very urgent" at the top there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does, but it is a very poor copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the copy that you have on your monitor.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that the handwriting belongs to the chief's secretary. I recognise her handwriting. And, yes, it does say "very urgent" just as it did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the contents of the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's going to be quite hard, but I do remember the important bits. Fine, well, we have the addressees up there, though this is also important. And what it should read, among others, is: To SJB, to all, to the chief. And the -- this is what I can try and make out. So to all the chiefs of all the stations. And I suppose to the police in Sarajevo, to the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here you are. You have a better copy there, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's so good that ... this is like the hieroglyphs. I'm really afraid that I'm going to make a mistake there. I don't remember particularly the heading. Why would I know? What I know is what the standard heading was. Normally there you would have the MUP there, the reference number and the date, and you can tell that there's -- the reference number is the latter part of it, 10-70, and the first few blots up there should be probably the MUP and the date. And the address. That's also important. So I suppose it says CJB, public security centre, all, meaning all in Bosnia-Herzegovina. SJB, all - chief. So all the municipalities, all the chiefs. And it used to be called the Sarajevo town SUP and then the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, for the convenience of the witness, now that we've gotten past the heading, the top part of the document that was not on the other version of the B/C/S, I don't mind if we put up in e-court or let him look from the hard copy that was originally shown to him which has the text from below "very urgent" on in a document that is more legible than the one that he is looking at. I'm satisfied that those texts are identical based on the English translation and comparing them. I think it would be easier for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, could you please, as it is one and the same document with the identical contents and the Prosecutor and I agree. I think it is more legible. In the document you have, the upper part is lacking, but please look at the contents.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. All right. It is the same. "I order," and everything down from there it's all legible to me. But what is at the top: "Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," number so-and-so, "I hereby order ..." So the minister is ordering it pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed as we can see on the screen. I remember that it was so. It was the then-minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Delimustafic. You can see it here on the screen. And here on paper that I have as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can I clarify? We don't have a signature on the screen. We have typed letters. Unless he's seeing something that I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's not visible. He just said signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let me explain this, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatches as a form of conveying information have, among others, the characteristic that a signature which is typed out like this has the weight of a real sign, a real signature and stamp because all the officers who work on encryption and encryption data protection were authorised officials just like any other authorised officials. We were not authorised as the police in order to bring people in and question them, but we had the responsibility for what we did. Therefore, if we made a mistake, I think that the penal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had Article 220, which envisaged a prison sentence between ten or even 15 years. So there had to be the words that it was signed by the minister and whoever received such a document or a dispatch as this one would know what I just told you. And for him, if an employee brought a dispatch as it is, would be the same as if the minister had signed it in front of him. I hope I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Mr. Jankovic, please have a look at the contents of the dispatch and tell me whether it is the contents which you saw on the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I cannot remember as precisely as that verbatim what stood there, but generally as I remember the document and its contents, I would say that what I read up here, it's all correct. If I should read it, I will read all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Please read it for yourself silently and just confirm for me whether the contents is the same in this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Block all the roads in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The units of JNA are pulling out materiel and equipment. This is to be completely blocked in direct coordination with the Ministry of Interior. Larger areas with military. I guess this word should be military installations but there is a typing error. From which they are trying to pull out materiel and equipment are to be blocked by using various manmade and natural obstacles. Yes, that's correct. That's the contents. Unannounced convoys of former JNA units and convoys without MUP escorts shall not be allowed to leave the barracks. That was what I termed block off the army. Prepare and begin combat operations. That's what meant that it was war for me. In the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina coordinate this with Territorial Defence Staffs in regions, districts and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the plans for combat operations. Plan widespread measures to protect the population. Yes, right. As far as I remember it was so. Perhaps there could be some minor details that are different, but it was like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you please have a look at the lower left-hand corner, the initials which are there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not easy to see but I know what it is. It says: DZZM. DZZ is actually the letter Dz from B/C/S in teleprinters, because DZ stands for the letter Dz because the machines do not have the diacritical signs above some of the letters so that the letter zh would be written as double ZZ. And the M, these are the initials of the communications officer who sent this from Sarajevo and I know who it was. His name was Mirsad Dzanko. This is why you have Dz M, for Dzanko, Mirsad. The communications officers, once they sent the dispatch, would include their own initials so that their colleague, if there was a need to make an addition or to correct something, he would know who to call. From Prijedor he would call Sarajevo, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of this communications officer, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the initials Dz M. Dz, if you know the letter, and it means Dzanko Mirsad. I didn't know him personally, but I remember all the names, including Mirsad Dzanko, from my work. I know him by name, but I didn't know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I ask counsel to clarify the spelling of that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I was trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please spell letter by letter the first and last name of this person? Please do it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. First of all, if you don't have the voice and letter Dz in your language, it's Dz like for dzamija, which is a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please no comments. Just spell it out.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: D-z-a-n-k-o, which reads Dzanko; M-i-r-s-a-d, which stands for Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. Can you please tell us, once you read the dispatch, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, it stands here Dzanko so perhaps you could use the same rule on our machines. DZZ so that it would then read Dzanko, but as you like. Can you now please repeat the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you read the text of this dispatch, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I said that I was shocked, but my work taught me not to do my job in accordance with shock but according to the rules of service. So knowing that this should be submitted to the chief of the station urgently, and I also knew that the chief was down at the meeting, and I needed to go down there again anyway, it was not my duty to do that. The communications officer who received the telegram would take the book, that was the rule. The book with telegrams. He would then note the receipt of the telegram in the book. He would take it, together with the telegram, to the person to whom it needed to it be handed. He would hand it over. The chief would sign in the book that he received it and the communications officer would bring back the book, so that was the proof that he handed the dispatch. So as the chief, I was not in charge of such duties but considering the urgency and that I had to go downstairs anyway and that the communications officers couldn't leave his room because he was alone there, I took the book, together with the dispatch. I went downstairs to the meeting and other communications officers whose superior I was were sitting together in one row. They were all equal among themselves. I addressed the first one who was the closest to me. It was Mirsad Sakulic [phoen]. It happened to be him. It was the person I talked about yesterday. I gave him the book, together with the dispatch, and I told him, Please, enter this dispatch and give it to the chief. And he did that. The course of the meeting was such that the meeting was already nearing the end. One could see that they had reached an agreement about what was proposed. That was accepted, as far as I could see, though I did not attend the second half of the meeting. And I then asked to speak for the first time in that meeting. I said that what they were promising, namely, that we would receive two salaries, was not correct. I said, Gentlemen, you're doing one thing and something else is happening. You're saying something and something else is going on. You are doing something else. I don't know exactly how I worded but I know that that was the thrust of my words. Those who should give us the money ordered us to go into war. And they asked me, How come you're saying that? And I said, Well, that's what it says here in this telegram. And then those present shouted, Read it out, read it out, because the chief already had the telegram in his hands. And then those who were present, the president of the municipality, the president of the SDA, Hasan and so on, they all came close together and they read it out in whispers. It lasted for perhaps four or five minutes. And other people were heckling and shouting, Read it out. Both Serbs and Muslims, as far as I could see. I didn't sort them and try to distinguish them from one another, but that's what I could see. And then after the consultations, the chairman decided that it should be read out and he gave it to Radovan Makecan [as interpreted], who was sitting there and keeping the minutes. Radovan Kecan. Excuse me, I'm very fast. And it has not been typed out. It is not Radovan Makecan, but Kecan. Right, that's it. He read it out, this dispatch, out loud. And all those present rose to their feet. There was disturbance. They were shouting at one and the same time. I just remember that the president of the municipality, Cehajic, was saying, It is a lie, it's an insinuation, it's not true. I'm leaving this meeting in protest. Dr. Mujagic, who was the president of the SDA, did the contrary. He was saying, People, sit down, let us reach agreement. It's not quite like this, and so on and so forth. However, there was no meeting anymore. Everyone got up and left. Should I add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, now that we're talking about the dispatch, where was the dispatch left?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan held it in his hand. It was addressed to him and given to him. Whether he took it with himself or not, I wouldn't know that. I don't remember what happened with it later. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have a chance, later on, to make another copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you now. It's the first time I see this. Here, on the dispatch I see on the screen before me there is something written in hand and it's the handwriting of Mira Topic, who was Hasan's secretary. And she was the one who would enter the dispatches in the book, so this seems to be a copy of that dispatch. But I don't know. Perhaps it is or perhaps not. I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether, after there was a takeover of power, you had a chance to make another copy of the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps two days after the takeover, maybe not on the very next day, I wouldn't know exactly, so perhaps after two days, Simo Drljaca called me to come downstairs, down to his office. I was on the upper floor. I came there, and there were one or two men sitting there. I don't remember anymore. And it's not important. He told me, These are the local journalists from the local newspaper "Kozarski Vjesnik." They want to write about this. Do you have that dispatch? I said, Chief, I personally have nothing, but I know that the communications officers, after the procedure of receipt, they had the yellow ribbons from teleprinter. They threw everything in a bag. I'm explaining that to you. I wasn't explaining that to him. They would put everything in a bag and later on they would burn it all, two or three days later, once the bag was full. So if I told them if they didn't burn it, then we might find it. I went down to the communications centre. I issued a duty to the present employees to try and find it and they did find it, the yellow ribbon, that was the trace from the dispatch. It hadn't been burned. So it could have been three days later. Because after that, the ribbon wouldn't have survived. It would have been thrown into the fire. The employees made a copy for me. I took it to Simo and gave it him, and he gave it to those journalists. I remember that a dispatch like this one was published in the newspapers. It was small, though, and it wasn't really legible, perhaps like this one, but it was printed there. And later on I wouldn't know what happened because I didn't follow it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, what happened after the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already after the end of business hours. It might have been 3.30 p.m., or maybe 3.00 p.m. As I said, people dispersed. Everybody went their own way. I went home. I spent time with my family because I didn't have anything particular to do. And then in the evening, although it was still daylight, but the sun was setting, my duty communications officer called me. By the way, whenever I was needed on an official business, they would never contact me directly. They would do that through the duty communications officer and he would locate me, and then I would call him back. Because that was the standard procedure to locate me because this duty communications officer was available 24 hours. Anyway, he found me and asked me to come over to the station. I went to the station, and I saw that there weren't many members of our service present. We were told that everybody should go to Cirkin Polje local commune, which is some 3 or 4 kilometres away from the entry point into the town. We were told that everybody must be there, including the police force, et cetera. I went there, but, of course, I left two of my workers behind in order to attend the centre and everybody else, including myself, went to Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived there, I can tell you that I saw quite a few people assembled there and amongst them were people looking in a variety of ways. People were dressed in old JNA uniforms, new JNA uniforms, camouflage uniforms, blue reserve police uniforms, proper police uniforms, et cetera. I knew some people from the regular police; whereas, I would say that 99 per cent of them I didn't know at all. And there was a total of them of approximately 150. They surrounded this building because, actually, this local commune was a pre-fabricated building. I entered the building. I found all the bosses and the commanders with whom I normally was in touch on a permanent basis in my line of work, and at around 8.00, when it was already dark, there comes a man whom I hadn't ever seen before. I heard of him, but I didn't know how he looked like. I didn't care. And he introduced himself by saying, My name is Simo Drljaca. He was in a military camouflage uniform, not the blue one, and he didn't have any cap on his head or any insignia. He said, I had been sent by the SDS, and from now on, I'm going to be the chief of station. All the executives from the police station were sitting there, minus the Muslims. But all the rest were there. Quite briefly, and without going into details, I saw that they were drawing up a plan, and the result was that they formed five groups made up of those people present, which approximately corresponded to two squads of 20 people each. I didn't go out to count the people, but, as far as I can remember, there were five groups of 20 men each, and each group was tasked of seizing all the vital facilities in the town, and amongst them definitely were the municipal building, the police building, the post office, the bank, and I think the court-house. I'm sure about the first two ones. Yes, there was a bank as well. The court-house and the post office. That's how it was. All of that was agreed. They went out, and then Simo asked me, Who are you? And I said, I'm a communications officer. What are you doing? I said, Nothing. He said, If that is the case, he gave me a piece of cardboard and it says "Official ID" on it. And he told me to write any name I wanted. I first wrote the name of Simo Drljaca. But people came to me. Because I didn't know them, they had to tell me their names. At 4.00 in the morning, they left because this whole procedure was lasting that long. Since it was dark, I couldn't see what was going on, and I wasn't interested anyway. There was no noise, there was no shouting. Everything was normal. After they left, at around 7.00, we were asked to go there. There was not a single bullet fired. We didn't hear anything to that effect. There were no signs of violence. At least as far as I was able to observe. I only heard from my communications officers who remained on duty, as well as the police who were on duty, that they were taken out of the building, and they were told that now the police of Republika Srpska, or, rather, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at that time, was taking over. They gave them some kind of ledgers or lists or whatever. Anyway, they were asked to sign the pledge of oath to the police that we used to do before anyway. And the people from my department didn't do that. They just went back to their offices and continued their work. But since that was happening at 7.00 in the morning, people were coming to work to the police, and whoever wanted to sign, they signed, and who didn't, they didn't. Those who signed proceeded to their workplace and continued to work as usual. Those who didn't sign was obliged to return -- turn in their official badge and their fire-arm. There were Muslims as well who signed this oath. I don't know how many. But I'm sure about a man called Enes, a Muslim, who worked in the same office with my wife. And there were a number of them as well, but I can't give you their names at the moment. I have forgotten them. As for those who did not want to sign, they were obliged, without any use of force, to return their official badges and their service fire-arms, and they were told that they were free to go, home or wherever they wanted. I didn't see it myself, but I heard from some of my co-workers the Muslims who refused to sign did not go back home on that morning, but, rather, assembled in a small park in front of a self-service restaurant which is about 100 metres from our building, and they were trying to draw up some plans of their own about what to do; but, as far as I know, they didn't make any attempts in that direction. And that is what happened on this first day, which was calm. I know that a young man called Dzapa, I think, was killed that day. That was the only casualty. He was a reserve police officer. He left the office and was headed home, and at a cross-roads, which is called Sacko's cross-roads in Prijedor, everybody knows where it is, and it's a busy junction, a bullet hit him on that spot. I don't think it had ever been established who fired that shot, but, anyway, he was killed. He was the first fatality. There were quite a few after that, but I remember him. So he was the first casualty in the aftermath of the takeover of power, and he was a Serb reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you when you spoke about the venue of the meeting held on the 29th of April. In addition to this hall, within that complex, in addition to the garages, were there any other rooms?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a high -- it's a -- it's a big facility. There are many rooms inside, and there was one office there where I sat and I didn't go out. But since lighting was very bad, quite a few of them were lit only if you had moonlight shedding light on these rooms. So I was asking myself, How come that I know nothing about it, whereas there were obviously huge preparations made ahead of it? There was a lot of SNB, or for the benefit of the interpreters that stands for olive-drab colour, and there were quite a few pieces of equipment of that colour which indicated that it belonged to the army. So there was a large amount of military equipment there, in addition to the camouflage uniforms that the army used and also the old army uniforms. Is that what you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one thing. But my second question was: In the SUP building, in this building, actually, in the yard, was there any other room?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's not so important at the moment, but when you enter this building, the hall is on the left-hand side, and on the right-hand side is a smaller room that previously was designed and constructed as a detention room. People were put in custody there by the police, and it had to comply with standards. There were no radiators allowed, et cetera, so this was a custody room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the public security station, was there any such detention room?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under the law that was in force before the war, every police station had to have such a room but we didn't have it inside the building itself. We had it in another building, and all the standards had to be complied with in order to prevent suicide of the detainees, et cetera. And the distance between the main building and that room was about, let's say, 20 metres, 15, 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any detention rooms in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not in the police building because there is no cellar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, just in order to get the chronology right, could you remind us when exactly the meeting that was called at Cirkin Polje and the subsequent takeover of the buildings in Prijedor, when did that take place exactly? On which date; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to give a more precise and more concise answer. I myself don't know anything about it. I know that the date was the 29th of April. As I said, I knew nothing about what was going to happen. The first I heard of the meeting was at around 1400 hours or, let's say, 1445. The dispatch arrives. I did what I did, as I explained to you. There was some commotion around 1500 hours, or 1515, after which I went home. And my house is about 1 kilometre away. I knew nothing about what was going on during that afternoon. As I said, I was spending time with my family. In the evening, or, rather, dusk, I would say that it could have been at around 7.00 or 7.30, that was the time when I was called to come to the SUP building, which I did, and then I went to Cirkin Polje, which is 3 or 4 kilometres away. We, from the communications service, took a Golf car. A driver drove us there, and then he went back so that we wouldn't have to walk over there. Let me tell you that Cirkin Polje is just a suburb of Prijedor. It looks like a village but it's a local commune that belonging to the town of Prijedor. So we come to this local administration building of this local commune, which was a prefabricated house. It has a yard that is the size of, let's say, three rooms of this size. So the sun was setting and, at that time, it was already pitch dark. I entered and what I explained took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to be -- to have confirmed that the takeover then, I understand, happened in the early morning hours of the 30th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And we're still on the 29th, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, of course, 4.00 in the morning, that was the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell us, please, after the takeover of power by the Serbs in the municipality of Prijedor on the 30th of April, in these early days, before the incidents that took place outside of Prijedor, were there any armed clashes in and around Prijedor? And I'm referring to the period before the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I need to recall the events, and the easiest for me to remember was what was happening at the station. As I said, there was this takeover of power. There were these first incidents, one of which was the one involving the death of a young man that I referred to. And the police began rounding up individuals and bringing them in for interviews more and more frequently. I wasn't privy to that. I can't tell you anything specific about it because I wasn't involved in it, but I do recall that this practice was on the increase. I can't even tell you specifically when exactly they took place. There were incidents before and after the period you mentioned. There were some incidents involving the killing of soldiers in Ljubija. They were killed by Muslims. I can't remember, really, at this point. It was tumultuous, but there wasn't fighting as such. If somebody refreshed my memory, I might remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, do you recall the conflicts in Hambarine and Jakupovici?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, Jakupovici does ring a bell. And not just those, there was Kozarac there as well. It's just that there was no police involvement in that. Well, I say that I heard about it, but -- and that there was no involvement of the police. Rather, there was the army. As for Hambarine, what I know is that they came across soldiers who were then killed. There's information in my mind that I can't be really sure of, that there was a car full of soldiers coming back from somewhere, were stopped at a check-point manned by Muslims. Something happened. They were killed. I don't know the date. I know that the check-points in the direction of Ljubija were manned by Muslims. I know that the soldiers who were killed were Serbs. I don't know the circumstances involved. Now you also mentioned Jakupovici. It's a large village, eastern-most in the municipality of Prijedor, in the direction of Banja Luka. One edge of the village lines the Prijedor-Banja Luka main road. Along that road, there travelled a column. I don't know who they were. Apparently there was an ambush of sorts. There was fire opened on a tank. The only thing I know is that a soldier by the name of Zgonjanin, from Prijedor, was killed. I don't know if anybody else was killed or wounded. I happened to know where that lad's house is, and I know that Muslims attacked a column passing by Jakupovici. The only thing I can tell you about still is about the radio station. That's what I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will be putting questions to you later on about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's the time for our break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take a break to return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let us resume. I was asking you about the incidents occurring in the last ten days of May. You mentioned Jakupovici, Hambarine, and Kozarac. In that period of time, did you have occasion to hear some of the conversations between the warring parties in your communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, between the 29th and the 30th of April and the 20th of May -- I apologise for using the term SUP all the time but that was the term that we used for so many years. So in the SUP, let me just tie all of this in. There was increased police activity, people were brought in and interviewed, and they were, in the main, people from Prijedor. However, Kozarac and its surroundings which were predominantly inhabited by the Muslims -- by the way, let me give you a piece of information that I came to know in my line of work, which was that the Kozarac substation covered 22.000 inhabitants. It is the size of two municipalities, in fact. And there was only a few Serbs and Ukrainians; the rest were Muslims. So this same Kozarac became directly inaccessible to the newly established authorities. The Muslims mounted their own barricades and placed their own guards. I don't know how -- how specifically it worked. I didn't go there. So any of us from the police force, when we had to go to Omarska, we took the route via Tomasica. For those you who are unfamiliar with the area, let me tell you that I have to take 25 kilometres straight, 25 kilometres to the right, and then back again, so I make this triangle sort of detour to go around Kozarac. Because it was quite evident that the new government was unable to have that area under control. Now, what I'm telling you right now were feelings that I had, not that I knew anything about it. This was one of the problems that the new authorities, the way I called them, it's not the official title, but to make things simple, this was one of the problems that the newly established authorities were confronted with. And this problem - meaning Kozarac - had to be resolved. They had their own leadership and their own senior officials who were consulted for things. It was an issue that went beyond the capabilities of the police force, and that's why the army was concerned with this. I didn't know much about it, but what I knew was that these people in Kozarac had their own staff or headquarters housed in what used to be the police substation or the police branch, and the only connections that they used to be in contact with the army was the ultra high frequency link normally used by the police, not by the army, because so far as I know, the army didn't have -- or the military equipment did not use that frequency. Thus, all these negotiations, or perhaps not all, there may have been direct negotiations, but a great deal of them took place over radio communications. In my communications centre, there were radio sets where one could overhear these conversations, and I did hear a few over the course of a couple of days. It wasn't the case, of course, that I was sitting there with my ear glued to that. I merely had an interest in having this matter resolved and would, on occasion, stop by the radio equipment to hear what the outlook seemed to be like. But this was more my personal interest. It wasn't something I did professionally. So I came to hear their commander, Osman Didovic, who used to be our commander, talk to them. He was -- or, rather, talk to Zeljaja. He was at the other end and he was the senior military officer in Prijedor. So Osman Didovic speaking to Zeljaja. Whenever said Zeljaja, Things have to be done this way, this is what we want, do this and that, Osmet would say, Well, I'm calling you from a vehicle. I have to convey your message to my colleagues and then we'll get back to you in an hour's time. The device I had in the communications centre had the ability of identifying the interlocutors because we would be able to tell by the number of the device used by the speakers. So I was able to tell that the device used by Osmet was no device used in a mobile facility such as a vehicle. Rather, it was part of their equipment in their station that they had over there. I didn't feel that I was best placed to go over to Zeljaja and tell him that what Osmet was telling him about where he was calling from was not true. I kept it to myself. And I'm saying it now. I don't know how significant it is. From what I know, over there in Kozarac they had their - how shall I call him? - man number one, man in charge, he was called Medunjanin or something like that. Or Medunjani. I'm not sure if he is from Kosovo originally. Just before the multi-party elections, he was in charge of national defence in the municipality. He joined them over there in Kozarac, and, from what I know, he was -- no, no, I'm not able to say what his title was because I don't know what his title was. So let me just say that he was the man in charge with them. So Osmet, when he was saying that he was going to convey this to other gentlemen, I could hear them because we had very sophisticated equipment in our centre. I could hear them whispering amongst themselves, so I suppose it was some sort of tactics that they employed. So this was how things went on for two or three days. They didn't manage to come to an agreement and the army set off for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let us just go back to Medunjanin. There is one bit missing in the transcript from what you said in your answer and I heard you say. Can you repeat, you said you didn't know what his function was but he was and can you tell us what he was exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't perhaps say this right. I don't know what the official title of that role was because it kept changing, secretary, chief, et cetera. From what I know, and I'm almost certain that after the multi-party elections he, or rather, the SDA, got the mandate for the position of the person in charge of national defence in the municipality. So let's say that that would be the equivalent in the municipality of the position of the minister of defence in the government. What exactly his function was, I don't know. And given the circumstances, he moved from Prijedor to Kozarac. Let me also say that they had carried out a sort of mobilisation of their own. After the military interventions that took place over there, I received from some of these soldiers -- well, easy come, easy go, I lost it somewhere. I received from one of those soldiers anyway, a tape with footage of their mobilisation. I was able to see fire engine sirens going off. They were running in all directions. Running toward the police station. Others were just walking in that direction. They gathered over there. I recognised a man by the name of Emir, who was a car mechanic and came to our station to repair our vehicles. I gave the tape to someone or lost it. At any rate, there's this one image I remember. My colleague Djuro Prpos, who I mentioned as having been present at the meeting, who was the commander of traffic police, well, this man was Djuro's brother-in-law. He was a JNA officer in Zagreb and came back. He was a Muslim, I forget his family name. So I saw him in this footage because he was a rather tall man of good physique. He had this camouflage uniform on and green beret with a crescent made of brass or something. He had a belt and tucked behind it he had a Heckler, the gun -- the rifle -- I mean, the pistol, you know. And he also carried a rifle. And there was some five or six of them outside the station and he came to them and said, Here I am. Allah is -- has given me the mission of doing you know what to Serb women and procreate young Muslims. And as we were watching this Djuro said, This is my brother-in-law. And the only thing I know of him is that he got killed in the subsequent fighting. And let me say that I have never told this to anyone before, this story. And the details I'm giving you now serve to put together the mosaic of it all. And even if the police had any role to play in it, it was so insignificant that I didn't know of it, and as the chief of communications centre, I had to know everything, every action that was being taken because I had to give them support from my end in terms of communications. And, of course, that fell onto me. So I can tell that you I didn't take part in any action, and none of the actions could have taken place without me doing appropriate communications work. So I have no knowledge of it taking place, and I have no basis to state that there were any policemen involved in the combing of the area covered by that Kozarac station. I heard that there were deaths on both ends, not many, but it was not an insignificant action. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us something about the events which took place on the 30th of May and the combat which occurred in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't told anyone but I wish to give you as good a picture of the situation as I can, to anyone who may be listening, and sometimes it may seem simple when you put into words. But one example is often very illustrative so I would give you one, if you allow me. It won't take long. The power changed hands. The SDS was in power. Now, according to the old system, the politicians are the ones who appoint managers, top officials, and so on. I was at the communications centre, and let me say that there were several rooms in it, and not everyone had access to it, including even the police employees. There was a key and there was a separation, as here. And I was sitting at my office. And one of my employees who was on duty at the time called me and said, There's a man who wants to see you. I came there, but I didn't know him. He told me, Are you the boss here? Yes, I am. Give me one Matorola - he didn't even know how to say Motorola and he meant the radio - and two batteries. I was looking at him and I could see that he did not have all his wits about him. Who are you, I asked him. He said, Don't ask me too many questions but just give it to me. I could see that there was something strange about that. So therefore, in order to be convincing I told him, You probably came to a wrong address. This is the police and the only thing can you get for free here is to be beaten. It is not really like that, but I was convinced that it was the only way to persuade him. And he did take that correctly. So he left. After that, I asked the other guy, Who was this? Maki Specijalac [phoen], he said. And this Maki, the special, was Marinko, a special, who had completed a special school for people with special needs and he was at the time holding the position of the director of all kiosks in Prijedor. But there was no single director or manager who was not appointed by the SDS. And who had appointed this Maki? It means that people who appointed him were not much better. And now a short break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't speak so fast.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope they will manage to record all this. I apologise. The point of all this is that a manager was somebody who was retarded and the main question is who appointed him? If these were the authorities that appointed him, then how could the other socially owned enterprises work, institutions, the police? What would the chief of police do if such a man came to see him? But he was sent by the person who appointed him so he would have to be respected. For me all that was questionable, but I told you this example in order to illustrate the situation that existed at the time. And now to go back to what you asked me. Namely, what happened in the latter part of this period between -- or, rather, up until the attack on Prijedor. As I said, the police summonsed some people, not too many. Those they termed the extremists and these were actually the Muslims who were holding higher positions in the organisation before there was a takeover of power. They questioned them but slowly, with a lot of inertia. I'm not sure where that was leading to. They also stepped up some sort of security and they set up some so-called check-points. They placed policemen to stand there on the roads that were leading into the town. Comment on one check-point and its fate. And that was just typical of the overall situation. You might know that was the check-point where we met for the first time, the Lepont cafe restaurant, and across the road from it there was one police vehicle and two -- or, rather, three reserve policemen. Three policemen. They just stood there. At the time everyone was very active, both the Serbs and the Muslims. Usually I don't mention the Croats because they were much fewer in numbers and no one paid too much attention to them. But, of course, they had their own beliefs, as all the people did. At the time, as I said, when everyone was carrying out activities in a hectic manner, whether these were important or unimportant activities, even the elderly ladies in the town who, I guess, were worried about their future, managed to attract attention. And it even happened to me that an old woman who just knew that I was employed in the police would tell me, Neighbour, I saw such and such a thing. Hoping that I would then inform the police about it, that in a certain spot -- because, for example, one old woman said, Neighbour, in Alija's house, and Alija was one of our colleague, a policeman, a Muslim, I saw that 14 men were in his house. I counted them through the window. At 2.00 they came out of their apartment. That was not a usual occurrence. It was interesting for this old woman and he would inform me about that. And that was all. So people paid attention even to insignificant things. Somebody else, never mind who, or, rather, I don't remember who it was, told me, and I heard from many sources -- I never asked him. There was just the information circulating. Everybody else would know that, not just me. Somebody knew more, somebody knew less about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I just ask where are we going with all of this. I should remind you, Mr. Krgovic, I should remind you that I think you have a little more than one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I asked you and I will ask you later about the general situation in the town, but let us return to the 30th of May and the attack on Prijedor, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. I'm sorry, I don't think I strayed from the situation, because all this information is connected with the attack itself. If I talked only about it, then it would seem that it came out of the blue. And that's not true. There were preparations ongoing. Let me just finish one sentence where you interrupted me. They told me that Dr. Eso Sadikovic travelled up every day to the hill, they meant Hambarine, and also one Cida, bringing equipment and all kinds of things up to the top of the hill so that the Muslims would organise themselves. The Serbs in Prijedor, at the station, heard that but they didn't do anything about, or perhaps they did somebody that was insignificant. And simply, on 30th May, at 4.00 a.m. in the morning, 4.00 a.m., no one expected that. There was shooting all around the SUP building and the court building. These days it was our duty, including myself, to be in the station building day and night. We had the right to go home to have a bath perhaps once in every three or four days. And it happened that that very night I went to my apartment, which is perhaps 1 kilometre away, in order to wash myself. And in the morning, when I was supposed to go to work, they called me and said, Cema [phoen] is shooting in the town. And my communications officers called me and said, Don't come here, because there's much combat going around, around the SUP building and the municipality building. And so I stayed there and waited for them to call me and tell me that I could get to the station. And I was only able to do so at 11.00. I later heard that the police was poorly armed and defended itself only up until the -- until 7.00, so that is to say between 4.00 and 7.00 a.m., from the building. And at 7.00 a.m. the army came along. It was assistance from them and I think there were one or two tanks. There was one for sure because I could see the cartridges and I also heard shots, perhaps one or two, not too many, but I'm sure I saw spent tank shell. So the army began fighting in order to separate them and push them back from the municipal and SUP buildings in a westerly direction, that is to say, towards the Raskovac suburb. And when they moved for about 500 metres, I was able to access the SUP building and then I joined everyone else from the communications service and remained there. The fighting went on in the town itself until the end of the day. It did not stop but they were moving away from the town centre. They went all the way to Ljubija and further, and I wouldn't know the details about that. That was already several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell me how many people were killed on that occasion? I mean, policemen.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first tell you that I have the number of 17 on my mind. I never had the need to try and remember that in any official manner. But that evening, when the fighting had already moved away from the town centre for perhaps 1 kilometre, Djuro Prpos, whom I mentioned, who was the commander -- or, rather, the deputy commander of the traffic police, called me to go with him to the Prijedor hospital. It was already at night. Perhaps at 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. I was to try and help him to recognise the policemen at the hospital morgue because the groups which were pulling out the dead and wounded didn't know who was a Muslim, who was a policemen or what. They just took them all there, the sick, the wounded, the dead, and it was necessary to recognise who was a Muslim, who was not, who was the attacker, and who was a member of our police, if I may put it that way. I don't know how many there were, but there were many, many bodies there. There were two rooms that were perhaps 10 by 6 metres, and they were laid out on tables and under them. Perhaps around 40 people. I recognised the ones I knew. I recognised all the active-duty policemen. And as for the reserve policemen, I didn't even know them. There were our people I didn't know and didn't recognise. I only recognised all the active-duty policemen, as many of them as there may have been. Perhaps four or five. I don't remember anymore. I remember that the little Lukic was there, Zeljko Ignjatovic, then Brane Jurtic [phoen] and so on. That's what I remember about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor and the conflict in Hambarine and Kozarac, did the security situation in Prijedor change in any way, and what sort of impact did that have on the work of the station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the biggest change, right then. Why? The units that had attacked, I never counted them, but as far as I know, the units which attacked on Prijedor were perhaps three or four companies. Three, I would say. Three, I guess. One attacked us from the factory. One from the bridge where we met at a cafe restaurant. And one from the east, from the area of Puharska. And Puharska is a local commune which belonged to the town. And, as I said, when the army and those who were chasing them began to push them back and they were withdrawing, there were those who withdrew and fled while fighting and there were many who surrendered themselves in one way or another. So that suddenly there was a huge number of these prisoners, if I can call them that. And then they detained those prisoners because they were so numerous. At first, what their plan was, as far as I could see, and I was present, they were to be treated as if one or two terrorists were caught in peacetime. They would bring him in, detain him and then process him. But as there were so many prisoners and the detention room was too small, I don't know how they had reached the agreement, I have no idea, but I remember that they began to collect them on the premises of the Keraterm company. Keraterm was a construction company. They had a big -- big hall but there were no machines so they found that as an appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say a company under construction what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a working company. It never really became operational. Someone found it and made it and put up the hall but there were no machines. And this was very appropriate because it was summer, not winter, this is the place where you could bring so many people. I only went once to Keraterm, perhaps for 20 minutes or half an hour, and I saw many troops, policemen, and whoever of all -- uniforms of all colours, but I just passed through and I glanced at them. I did not really observe anything because I didn't need to. All I remember is this sight that I saw of many people dressed in various uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that -- it was something that I didn't know much about. I only once went to Keraterm to fix a telephone. But then I heard that they were short of space due to the large number of detainees, and they wanted to move to a bigger premises in the Omarska mines. And that's the first time I heard of it, and I went there. On that day, I don't know when it was, when the first prisoners were taken to Omarska, it was 1800 hours, and I remember that precisely because Simo, my superior, called me and asked me, Do you have any available radio sets? You need to establish a connection urgently. And I said, Yes, I always have an emergency radio set available. He asked me, Can you go to Omarska and install that? I looked at my watch. It was 6.00; I remember clearly. He told me, Go there. You will find our policemen up there. Tell them that you need to install a radio set, and they will tell you where to do that. Of course, I took the device with me and a technician and an official car. On that day, one had to travel to Tomasica, so one had to bypass Kozarac for security reasons, although via Kozarac was a much shorter way. When we arrived, it was still daylight, but darkness fell soon thereafter. I found our policemen there who -- who were members of the Omarska police squad. Among them, I remember seeing Miroslav Kvocka, who was here later on. I remembered him because he was a neighbour of mine in Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have much time, can you briefly tell us how long you stayed there and when you went back.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right. So I installed the radio set. I made it operational. It was already darkness. I was -- wanted to go back. The police told me that I couldn't leave at that time because the buses with the detainees were just arriving, and it was not advisable that I travel in the opposite direction. Therefore I parked my vehicle some 100 metres away until this whole operation was completed. Then we travelled at around midnight back home. We came across the Serb check-point and it was towards the dawn when we reached Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When was the second time you went there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when they had some broken-down telephone line, and again I went with a technician there. I have to tell you that this whole facility had only one telephone line. That was in the office of the secretary of the former company manager. I fixed this broken telephone line. We didn't spend more than 20 minutes on the job, and we went back. And the third time was when two people at the police station in Prijedor, actually, two servicemen, a captain and a staff-sergeant, approached me, and they both spoke in the Ekavian dialect which was predominant in the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this wasn't quite clear. Who these people were membered of?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were in the army uniforms. I don't know to which unit they belonged. I never asked them. They were from the army, they were outsiders, not from our region judging by their accents. Maybe they were just attached to this unit in Prijedor. I perceived them to be some sort of military investigators. And they asked me, they did not request decidedly, they just asked me to go with them to Omarska as a kind of professional who would accompany them there, as a kind of expert to accompany them. When I understood what their request was, I said, yes, I was prepared to help them, because I always want to help people. But I told them that I will not discuss anything else with anyone there except the things that have to deal with this particular piece of equipment. Because that was without my scope of responsibility. My sole responsibility had to do with technical issues, and as an engineer, it was my duty to assist them. And they didn't ask for more, to be honest, and that's how it happened. They brought two men and started questioning them in turn. One of them was an elderly man, looked like a farmer, and the other one was a rather well-off owner of equipment for logging. I don't know what his name was. They were allegedly accused of buying a radio set for the Muslims, and he was a Muslim. The other one was called, I think, Mihajl. He was a teacher from Lamovita, from the elementary school there, and he was accused of allegedly operating this radio set to communicate with Kozarac and to tell them that a unit from Banja Luka was on its way. They were questioned for about half an hour. Being someone who is not versed in these issues, I thought that they were quite innocent. The first one said that somebody came and that he was asked to sent a message to Kozarac, an encoded message, a wedding party is passing through, and that referred to this unit that was heading for Kozarac. Soon thereafter they admitted to having done that, to having this radio set --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing that wasn't recorded. I heard you say that this one reported which kind of unit was coming from Banja Luka? Police or army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An army unit. And that happened approximately at the time when this young man Zgonjanin was killed. I suppose it was an army unit with one or more tanks because I remember that a tank came under attack. Anyway, this man called Nihad perhaps, I'm not sure, his -- their communications officer, if I can call him that, sent this coded message which read: The wedding party is passing through. And this interview lasted only until the point when they admitted to the location of the radio set and this radio set is -- appeared to be -- to have been hidden in a nearby house. I went there with them. We found this little house. And in a wooden stove, we found the radio set. However, when we -- actually when we looked there, we couldn't find it, but we found only cables for an Accu battery. That was indicative, obviously, of the fact that a device used to be there. And not far from that point, there was an old point where some elderly Serb peasants set up their check-point and all the uniforms that they had was some ancient SNB reserve military uniforms. They didn't deny things for a long time. They admitted to this very quickly. They told us about the house. And when we went there, we found the mother and the wife of this man called Dusko. He wasn't around, and after some threats were made, the radio set was handed over. I took the radio set and I realised that it was a rather new type of CB radio set.
