CB stands for civilian band which is a radio set that the can be used by anyone without a licence throughout Europe. That was in the era before mobile phones. So one did not need any licence or permit to either purchase this set or to use this. That was the only type of radio set that was allowed to be used. They took the radio set with them, and I never heard of them again or discussed this issue with them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: These people where this radio set was found and confiscated, what was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Serbs from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I'm going to move to another subject now. And it has to do with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to me because we have to go back to something. I don't know if I understood you correctly. Whose radio set was it and how come that it was in the hands of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how? This communications officer Nedzad said that it was in this road by the Prijedor-Banja Luka road. This was their communications centre, if I may call it. And he hid it underneath the oven in this stove which means that he wanted to conceal it and to come later to fetch it and use it again. In the meantime, the situation changed because Serbs came after the Muslim attack to guard this point. These were those elderly Serbs. They even had some rifles, M48 rifles from Second World War. And they were all so-called old timers, both them and their rifles. Just like all nosey people, they looked around this house and they discovered the radio set, and they took it away, because people thought that anything is worth taking away. And that's how had came to be in their hands. That was just greed. There was no organisation behind it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That was just greed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was personally a greedy person. If I had seen that radio set, I wouldn't have taken it, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let's go back to the operation of the Prijedor police station prior to the outbreak of conflict and the time when Simo Drljaca was appointed SJB chief. Did anything change in the mode of operation of the public security station? What was his methodology and how did he run the station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of power and at the outset of the conflict in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now it's clear. Everything started in a stormy way. Starting with the events surrounding Keraterm. Then the emergence of Omarska. There was almost no practice that was pursued before, in terms of the chief having us in his office and reporting to him. It was only individuals who went to Simo's office. They were agreeing things. I also went to see the chief whenever I needed to ask him something, but more and more frequently, his secretary was telling me that I couldn't get in because someone was in a meeting with the chief. So I was pushed aside more and more. There were fewer and fewer people with whom he conducted these so-called operative activities that had nothing to do with police work. I don't know what I was supposed to do with that situation. I just could make suppositions. People were coming and going. And you know better than I do what was going on when you talk with those people. I was not interested much in that. But this operation of this particular police station was far, far from normal. That's in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jankovic, what was the situation on the streets of Prijedor? Was it safe?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, far from it. In the town of Prijedor and in the general area, the situation was extremely chaotic. Some wanted to seize somebody's house because people had fled and abandoned their property. People were starting to drink. Some other people started developing all sorts of ambitions of becoming heros or what. Others, as I said, took to binge drinking. There was a man who -- and I'd like to tell you this. There was no organised shooting by the Serbs at the Muslims. In the evening I was at the SUP building. It was still daylight, and I went to a house where my children were being minded by a woman and there was a man standing on the carriageway by -- close to the curb. He was in a military uniform and there were another two men in the civilian clothes talking to him. There was no one else around. When I was passing by, one of them called me, Hello, you, big head. And I turned towards him, and he said, Yes, yes, I'm addressing you. Are you a Balija? Which is a derogatory name for Muslims. And I said, No, I'm not. He said, Show me your ID. Now let me tell you this. At that moment I had my ID, I had my police ID, I had my fire-arm with me, but I decided that in spite of that, the best possible approach was -- would be to show him my papers in a peaceful manner. He looked at it and there was the old name of the village where I was born, which was Zabar, and he read this, and he swore at me, saying, Oh, you are from Zabar. And then he took out his pistol and fired a shot at me. He missed me by this much from my right leg. There was a big linden tree behind me. I could have jumped behind its trunk and shoot him dead but that would require too much investigation and proving on my side. I saw that he was under the influence of alcohol. His eyes were bloodshot, and these two started wrestling with him in order to grab the pistol off him. So I decided that the best policy would be for me to withdraw and leave it be. This is just an illustration of what was going on in the town at the time, irrespective of your ethnicity, of your background, whatever. There were all kinds of motivations and all sorts of negative traits came to the surface. So this was resembling more a chaotic situation and there was no -- any thought for organisation. I was not the only such case. The daughter of Zoran, a Serb, was fired by someone. She was shot with a bust of bullets and she was raped as well. So I won't go into that. Total chaos. So everybody who was an ordinary person tried to avoid moving around the town, and I restricted my movements only to the things that had to do with my duties and job. I didn't go for a stroll.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we're discussing reporting, I have a document I want to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P00374. That's behind tab 2 of the Zupljanin Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have tab 2 in a photocopy there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to do there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document. The document is instructions on reporting. Have a look at page 2 and the signature block which reads: Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Herein, Mr. Zupljanin reads as follows -- writes as follows: "Every day reporting on daily activities of the CSB Banja Luka coming from the various stations is riddled with faults and shortcomings as follows ..." Do you have the document there before you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then follow as I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it 0043234? So that is dispatch 11-0-11, 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And the first sentence which reads that the reporting is riddled with shortcomings. And under 2 it reads: "Not all important events are reported on. Frequently information is not complete. Morning dispatches are not sent out in a timely fashion. The events which are learnt of subsequently are not recorded and incomplete reports are sent out. Supervisory staff barely check and supervise any these reports."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: What sort of situation prevailed in Prijedor when it comes to reporting? Could this be said to apply to Prijedor as well when it comes to the reports that were being sent out?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Prijedor was practically inefficient. Let me explain. This sort of dispatches were textbook dispatches, and requests were sent for dispatches to be corrected if they went out of the ordinary format by 5 per cent. Now let me tell you that what happened in this period of time was that illiterates came to work for the SUP so you -- the dispatches couldn't be said to deviate by 5 per cent on what was the ordinary dispatch but by 95 per cent. And attempts were made to remedy this, but I think it was not really within his ability. I haven't had occasion to read such documents as this one before, but as I look at it, I can see that the situation in Prijedor had nothing to do with what was proper police work. Incompetents came to work. Simo Drljaca used to be a lawyer, I think, and I think he worked for a music school and I think he also worked in this local government department for education. And then can you imagine? A lawyer working in a music school and then coming to work for police? His level of knowledge was nil. When you come to a police station and you see a duty officer behind his desk, and next to him some ambitious men like Zdravko Torbica, these were people who had high pretensions but were practically illiterate. Plus, they had no sort of support from Simo. He didn't force them to do their job properly. Their reports did pass through my hands because they went through the communications department, but I didn't read them. I'm sure there's as many as 50 of items in this document that were not really addressed in everyday work, and I don't think even five of them may have been covered in everyday work, and if they were, they were probably worded in an illiterate manner. I hope my answer was sufficient for your purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear. Mr. Krgovic didn't switch his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see, you said a moment ago -- you said that they were illiterate in police terms. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I coined that expression, if I can say so. It doesn't really exist. Let me explain, well, illiterate in police terms. He was ignorant of the basic police work. They didn't know that they were supposed to receive tasks from the superiors and report back to them on the tasks accomplished, that Simo had to have problem information from his subordinates and had to properly inform his superiors thereof. He didn't know that. His superior was the chief of centre and he was supposed to report to the chief of the centre. He never did so. He got hold of a position of power, and he probably thought that the chief, as well as gods, were beneath him. In other words, basic policing duties that every policemen ought to have been aware of were not something that any of the incumbent policemen knew. And let me tell that you not of all of them were as incompetent as that. There were people working in the police force before and couldn't work in ways that weren't prescribed by standard procedure because they had come to learn it. Of course, quite a different issue is what sort of influence these people who were literate in police work were able to wield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, in your evidence so far, you said that there were difficulties in the payment of salaries. Can you tell us, in this period prior to these events, who did the police receive their salaries from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality. Well, I say "municipality." We know what it is. There's also the party organisation, the SDS. However, in reality, they were people who were municipal functionaries as well as SDS members. They sent one of their own lot, that's to say, Simo, to take charge of our duties. They had their own plans that they tried to put into effect through Simo and us. And, of course, they paid us our salaries. In the previous system, during Yugoslavia, there was local administration, and the SUP received their salaries from the municipality. So in that sense, not much had changed with the new government. They knew that it was the municipal revenue that served to pay for municipal justice administration, police, schools, et cetera. And, in fact, even I myself had to obey what they had to say, not directly, but through Simo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From what I understand, you did not feel that this power was being exerted directly to you. Rather, through Simo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They would approach Simo and give him a task and, of course, as part of the police force, I was duty-bound to perform the task. And it was never the case that Simo received a task from them that had solely to be performed by the communications department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The influence wielded by the municipal government, was it something out of the ordinary to you, something that did not exist in the previous period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, far from it. In the former Yugoslav system, we had the municipal committee of the League of Communists, and whatever they said had to be done was done. And, of course, the chief of the police station would go there to learn what he had to do. Now it wasn't the League of Communists any longer. Now it was the SDA, and Hasan would go there to get his instructions on what he was supposed to do. Then it was the SDS, and Simo had to go over there to learn what it was that he to do. So that's how the situation changed in just under a year. Eventually, as the government grew stronger, things changed. We received our salaries from the republican levels, as well as orders, et cetera, but it took time to get to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document now. Or, in fact -- yes. Let's look at it briefly, P00621.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number is it? 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Report on the work of the Security Services Centre Banja Luka. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of July until the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have several minutes before we take our break. So please take the document with you over the break and have a look at what it has to say, and then I'll put a couple of questions to you after the break. We are nearing the end of my examination. So please have a look at page 21, 22, and 23.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take it with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let me just find it. You mean the typewritten 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 21 through to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I intend to move onto my last topic, or one of the last topics in my examination, so perhaps we should take the break now so that the witness may have an opportunity to review the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. We will take the break and return at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When we took the adjournment a little before 12.05 and I said we would return at 12.25, I thought that the extra three minutes would have been sufficient for the business that the Chamber knew it would have to do. We apologise to everyone for the inconvenience of a break that has extended long beyond what we anticipated. But we -- we -- we spent the time trying to solve a problem with which Mr. Zecevic is immediately concerned. It's in the process of being worked on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have 20 minutes left to finish my examination. As I have lost quite a lot of time to clarify some issues, I would ask you for additional time until the end of today's session, if possible, so that I could complete all the topics that I have discussed until now. That's about 40 additional minutes. I have talked to the Prosecution and Mr. Cvijetic and they do not oppose this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed. We would only ask your assistance, Mr. Krgovic, in getting the witness to focus on answers to -- you know, without wandering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I gave you these documents to read. But before you -- before we get to the document I forgot that we need to clarify a few things in the transcript because we overlapped while speaking. You talked about your visit to Omarska, and as you were approaching Omarska, who was securing the part where the prisoners were and also the road leading to Omarska itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I once saw when the telephone was repaired, that was my second visit, around the building, there was a concrete slab that was 15 or 20 metres wide, perhaps from here to that wall, and the prisoners or the detainees were all there. It was really hot and they had a hose with water, and they were splashing one another in order to cool down. And around that was a grassy field with a few trees and bushes, and young men in military uniform were standing in the shade and they had light machine-guns, M53, from the JNA. These were light machine-guns with ammunition. They lay down. And at the entrance were two such men. And as I was passing through, it was really unpleasant. Two light machine-guns would be pointed to you and I told them, Well, if anyone made a disturbance now would you shoot? And they said, Yes, of course, we would. And I said, Well, here I am. And they said, Never mind, you are together with the others. And the light machine-gun, as the weapon, was something that did not exist among the weapons that the police had at its disposal. It's a piece of combat equipment. I know it from the JNA. It was the army that had it. Who these men belonged to, which unit, I don't know. But I'm sure that they were not policemen, at least judging by their uniforms and by the weapons that they had. I didn't analyse that any further so I don't know who they were and which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, when you talked about the meeting held in the night between the 29th and 30th, you mentioned something that has not been recorded. How did the majority -- what did the majority of the people wear? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a motley crew, all sorts of uniforms, all sorts of colours, camouflage, military, then the old olive-drab JNA uniforms, as I said, then police uniforms that the reserve police forces had. These were the blue ones of poor quality. There were active-duty policemen in their own uniforms, so everything was represented. I didn't count but there were perhaps 150 or 200 men. The police station itself couldn't have had so many employees. There were many others there. Those were those who were not uniformed, who were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any army officers present?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two officers came. Everyone was looking for me and wanted to get a Motorola. I don't know who it was, a major by rank. It was the first time I saw him. He asked for two radio sets and batteries. I asked him, Who are you? And he said, I am a major. Major, you're wrong, I said. I have no majors on my list. I just have policemen. And he left and never looked for me again, but he didn't get what he wanted. These were the two officers. There may have been others but these were the two that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us the rank of these officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who requested a Motorola was a major. As for the other one, I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you now please look at the document which I gave to you. That is P00621. I asked you to look at page 21 but I will ask you also to look page 20 before that. That's the previous page. It's typed out, the page number 20.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court in B/C/S, it's page 43, and also page 43 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't get what you said. Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it has nothing to do with you. It's in the upper right-hand corner page 20, and I'm interested in the second paragraph from top. It's the report from the centre which says: "Inefficiency, lack of professionalism and superficiality of work in a number of SJBs contributed to a large extent to the functional detachment of a number of SJBs from the centre. This has gravely affected the overall unity and the social role of the security organs and services. Parallel to that, some of the SJBs connected themselves with the local politics and local political leaders, thereby neglecting their legal obligations and authorisations. Namely, the top-ranked staff of some SJBs, instead of keeping a highly professional attitude towards [sic] their work, occupied themselves with issues which are outside of their remit." And then - let me not read the whole paragraph: "Their intention was to avoid responsibility for what has been done and to lay it on others. But various concessions have also been made under the influence of those organs and individuals at the expense of the service, that is to say, of the law ..." Mr. Jankovic, Mr. Zupljanin is here discussing certain occurrences. What I read out to you from this paragraph, does this illustrate the situation which existed in Prijedor? In light of everything I have read to you, does this correspond -- I apologise because this is perhaps too long and suggests it was a leading question so I will try to reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to say anything. I understood from what you asked me and what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have an objection, first, that it was leading but also I think there's a lack of foundation for this witness to answer the question so far. In terms of what he's said about Mr. Drljaca, he talked about how he really didn't have much dealing with him, that Mr. Drljaca was cutting him out more and more, that he saw him meeting with people unspecified as to who these people were. Without some further foundation, I don't know that he is in a position to express a meaningful opinion to you regarding this. Unless there's some further foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I confess, I've lost what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never asked it, Your Honours. I just read this. And when I saw Mr. Hannis on his feet, then I could see that the first half of the question was not satisfactory so I stopped before asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, there is an assessment given in this report by Mr. Zupljanin. Can you tell me, when we talk about Prijedor and the relations and how everything functioned, can you comment for us on the situation in Prijedor in terms of the relations between the Security Services Centre and the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first tell you that I read this, and I thought about this while I was sitting in that room over there. What is written here, what I can see here, is -- was much, much worse in Prijedor - I don't know about other places - than as it is stated here. Yes, that was the character of things but it was much worse in Prijedor. And let me tell you what I said and what Mr. Prosecutor, who is to the right of me, said, that I was left out. It was not just me. Everybody else from the town was present all along and they felt that in a thousand ways. One could feel that there was anarchy and many individuals had a wish mainly to become rich and to do other things that were not allowed. There were policemen who abused their positions, who imposed conditions. For example, what a policeman could have used, they would help someone who wanted to flee not to do it in a legal manner. If people wanted to move out and go to Europe or somewhere. It is known now what the way to do that is. You need to have a travel document and so on. So a policeman would use the uniform and the official ID and everything. He would take money from the person, drive him through ten police check-points, and they would let him pass. So this was a well worked-out system. It wasn't something that was not visible. The citizens could see it and feel it on their own skin. And Mr. Zupljanin writes here about that, inter alia. But, still, let me know -- let me not be too extensive but it's the same like when I told you about what was in the previous document. This is how the superiors used to write that even previously, but previously you would have five criminals in two groups and there would be an activity carried out by the group, and now it was the other way around. Five per cent of people were not criminals, and now the question is how efficient the service can be. We can see from his attempts and how he tried hard and he wanted to rectify the situation and one cannot say that there were no results. Unfortunately, although on the other hand, luckily, the situation did not last too long, nothing much could have been done, and I wish that Simo had informed me in a better way about this. So would you like to hear something more about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about reporting, it says here that: "Regularly a number of SJBs are ignoring the requests from the CSB to address certain issues, that is to say, that the requests from the centre remain unheeded, which jeopardises the unity and -- of the organs as a single security mechanism. Under such circumstances it is difficult to keep the total security situation under control, to evaluate and make valid security estimations at the level of the region and the republic." Mr. Jankovic, while you were working as a communications officer at the communications centre, you knew, given the quality of the communication equipment that you had and the quality of the people that you had working in the centre, how did this process of exchange of information between the SJB and the CSB go?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a minute ago when I spoke about political illiteracy, every member of the centre from the lowest level to the highest level should have known how to receive the tasks and how to write reports.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start all over again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, did the witness hear the interpreter's request?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please, since the interpreters didn't manage to follow what you were saying, can you please repeat your answer that you gave to me. I'm sorry, we didn't get an interpretation, so can you please repeat what you told us about the process of sharing information, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to your question, but since I spoke about this topic many times in the past, when I gave statements to the Prosecution and elsewhere, maybe can you find it there. Maybe you're referring to that. I'm going to repeat what I said before. I said there were many things there involved, and I'm going enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Initially, people didn't know that they had to report, so they failed to report. Report to whom? Report to your superior. Not only report but send him proper information and reports. After this, the senior officers knew that they had to report, but they didn't have any interest of their own, because they had their own private vested interests not to do that, including some internal policies that were detrimental to the service itself. Now, what does this have to do with communications system? Well, it has a direct link with this, because that was the worse time for the communications system, due to the lack of power, due to the lack of spare parts and faulty equipment. However, even when there was communication, people would resort to such excuses by saying, You know, Boss, I tried to get in touch with you but the communications system was down and I failed to send you a report. What I'm trying to say, people were trying to blame the communications system for everything because that was the most convenient excuse that they could have resorted to when they wanted to evade something. Now if this is the answer to your question regarding the communications system, fine. If you need additional information, please tell me so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, there is some ambiguity in the interpretation here. You said when somebody wanted to evade something. Who was it who wanted to avoid sending a report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every member of the police from the lowest level up to the level where Simo was; I'm talking about Prijedor only. I'm not going into the ministerial levels. If there was a need for him to deceive his superior, they found a cunning way of blaming the communications system for such failure. I'm not inventing this. For example, there was a policeman who simply would cut off the cable of the microphone or to cause a shortcut to occur. As the head of this department, I introduced a rule in order to -- to stop this. For every device that is being brought to us to be repaired, if some malfunction happened normally, then the technicians would fix it. However, if it was damaged, then the policeman, through his commander, should report to me and should confirm whether this was damaged on purpose or not. I'm talking about ordinary police officers, but even the bosses were not immune from that. If they wanted to find some kind of excuse, they would say, Oh, the system was down. Maybe this was due to some totally mundane and trivial reasons, but that's how it was. But I didn't try to fight this when it comes to those senior officers, as I did try to find -- fight this practice with the ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, after the outbreak of hostilities and the commencement of fighting in Prijedor, can you tell us what the communications was like in Prijedor. What did you have at your disposal? What kind of communications devices did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the outbreak of hostilities and all these events and the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as these tumultuous times proceeded, the system was not harmed too much. However, it was persistently being hampered by the loss or disappearance of devices. But for the most part, the most harming was that of the power outages. In that period, as far as the operations activities were concerned, there was a VHF [as interpreted] radio communication. It shouldn't be VHF. If you want to have it in English, it should be UHF. Not very high frequency but, rather, ultra high frequency, UHF. All right. So we had this UHF system for operative purposes, and for the transmission of written information, we still used teleprinters with their in-built crypto protection systems and all the devices that go with it. However, now, the flow capacity of those systems was dramatically reduced. Why? Because of the lack of electricity supply. Secondly, this system used transmission routes of the general telecommunications system, what we used to call the post and telegraph and telephone. And we were simply just users of some of their channels. And once those channels are cut off, we lose them as well. Now that given that much, much earlier, before we faced these difficulties, we had a communication line between Prijedor and the neighbouring municipalities such as Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica. Then we had a connection upwards, hierarchically speaking, that is towards the Banja Luka centre, and then further on towards the republican MUP. That was a normal state of affairs, and nobody changed anything in that organisational system. Now, with the emergence of all these difficulties, the damage to the channels that we experienced, some experienced more problems, other experienced fewer problems, the connections with Banja Luka was partly operational, but as soon as we were cut off from electricity supply, or if the post office was affected in the same way, then everything breaks down. However, as for Sarajevo, that was a long way away. There were a long [as interpreted] of channel joints and connections there, and I don't think that later on, nobody even bothered to try to send any dispatch. Maybe at the beginning, but later, never. We used fax machines to convey and relay written information because we still had a telephone line operational, surprisingly. So it was somewhat difficult to pass on information to the republican SUP somewhere in Sarajevo, or close to Sarajevo, Pale, I presume, but I know that, as for Banja Luka, I can't give you the exact percentages, because it went up and down. The volume of communication was reduced, and the exchange of information was getting more and more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In comparison to the pre-war period, before the conflict, and if you compare the number of incoming and outgoing messages, what was the percentage of the successfully transmitted outgoing messages in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It varied as well. You know how it is. Before, in peacetime, we could manage to send the dispatch very quickly. People were entitled to have eight hours to do that but they would do it immediately. Now, however, there was a two- or three-day's delay for even those of the most important dispatches. It was impossible to send them. There was one dispatch, for example, that I myself saw. It was shown to me by a gentleman from the OTP when I gave statement to them, and there's my signature on that dispatch as well. And it speaks volumes about what I'm talking about now. And if you can find it, I can comment on it, and it really speaks a lot about the question that you have just asked me. I don't know the contents of it. But I know that there's my signature there and it's circled. This dispatch would be immensely helpful in answering the question that you asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jankovic, concerning the links with other centres that ran over the territories that were controlled by the Muslims, was it possible to use them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These communication lines towards Banja Luka travelled entirely over the Serb-controlled territory. Therefore, there was no trouble in that respect. There were, however, some cables that, for example, were laid next to the railway tracks and for a period of time, this cable was damaged so we have to -- had to use a bypass connection. Now, as for the links with Sarajevo, only God knows how it happened. I don't know how it operated. Vlasic was one of the hubs and I know that there is a repeater at Mount Vlasic and I think, for a time at least, it was in the Serb hands, maybe I'm wrong. But there are other summits that were never in the Serb hands. You know, war has changed all the routes that existed before. I wasn't involved in that, but other people know about that. The only open communication line we had at the time was via fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that all these routes disappeared. It was not recorded. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant that the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was covered by a proper network of communication lines that the police used before the war. However, at various places, various things happened, such as fighting, or this, or that, which would damage one communication link. It becomes severed. Then they tried to find another route. So eventually there were so many severed links that we were virtually cut off, except for the fax, as I told you. I related this to the people from the ATP. There was just one case, where a fax was sent to director -- just tell me -- I'll tell you briefly about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There's no need to go into that. We've already explored this area. Tell us, were there difficulties experienced with that particular line as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fax line you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it so happened that it was impossible to get the number that you dialed. It required perseverance. At times, it took 20 minutes to get connected, and at times, it was impossible. You'd dial a number, and the line would be silent. And, thus, for many more attempts, until you get the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, you say that, in order for the communications system to be up and running, you had to have electricity to power it. What was the situation in terms of power supply in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were frequent power outages. The longest period we went without any power was 40 days. Now the post office had its own power generator. I improvised and made a makeshift system that hooked onto that generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have very little time left so can you please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it would so happen that we have power at times; at others, we didn't. It was in stops and starts. That's how it went. The same was true for the spare parts that we had a shortage of. There were difficulties from every quarter. I didn't keep an exact record of how many dispatches were able to be transmitted. On average, I could tell you that one-third of transmissions were successful. But that's just a rough estimate on my part. This was largely due to the fact that many of the links that had been operational before did not work anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the system of dispatches, of telegrams, in fact. What was the procedure applied as soon as a dispatch arrived at the MUP, where would it go before it reaches the person it was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a dispatch arrives in, you can tell whether it's open or protected. That's to say, coded. If it's coded, then the communications officer would decode it. There were four ledgers or books. You had open dispatches received; protected dispatches received; open dispatches transmitted; coded dispatches transmitted. So if you receive a dispatch you look at whether it is open or protected. Then you place it in the appropriate ledger. It goes with the filing service. They will file exactly the time and date of arrival. And that's -- and then it's handed over to the person it's addressed to. Likewise, if you have an outgoing dispatch, then you have the person bringing in the dispatch to the service. It's filed in the book. The communications officer places his signature to prove that he has received it. He transmits it on. And his job is done. Now, the form of the dispatch, let's say you have -- you have a dispatch that comes in. You send it, you transmit it. And then the communications officer would not keep it with him unless there was a correction coming from the other end. And then if there's no such correction, he would merely return it to the person who brought the dispatch in to be transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the books or ledgers that you mentioned. Or the filing books. Were they books belonging to your department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You see, the communications system was organised in such a way that we had books, the pages of which were of a specific format. For instance, Sh 19, Sh 12, those were specific forms and they had different columns. Columns for dispatches received; for dispatches transmitted, et cetera. They conformed to the rules introduced by the JNA. You see, the cryptographic data protection that a country would use would be normally the one chosen by the army. Of course, we only used a part of the system. The system was partly also used by embassies, for instance. So we were given these rules by the JNA and had to adhere to it in our work, and this applied to the books as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us, was there an obligation to store these books; and, if so, for what periods of time, for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coded books were supposed to be kept for up to a year. And the open ones would be destroyed upon the expiry of six months. You see, these books be used up very soon. Normally, you wouldn't destroy a book that hasn't been filled. If it is only half full, then you'd probably use it again for the next time-period. Or, if it is almost full, then you'd destroy it and take a new book. We drew up reports, as at the 25th of December, that was the date, the cut-off date, and that was normally then the date when we changed all these things. Of course, you also had reports for the trimester and half year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was this standard procedure which was applied both in the pre-war and the post-war periods?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That procedure was in place before my arrival there. I applied it. It was used in peacetime. These books are not taken anywhere normally, so you can't really misplace them. They're always on the desk or kept in a safe. Of course, it wouldn't be just the books that would be kept in a safe. You'd have coding material there. And then if you've got up to 15 books in there, you wouldn't be able to fit anything else. And you were then forced to destroy them, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, lastly, tell me this: At the start of your testimony, I asked you about the sightings of Mr. Zupljanin in 1992. So did you see him anywhere in Republika Srpska in 1992, as you assumed your duties there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the month of November, as we were heading for Orasje. Or, actually, it was November -- well, I don't know the date. I think it was November. It was an organised trip. We had the police force from Sanski Most, Dubica, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Gradiska. There were many of us. We gathered in Banja Luka. If I remember correctly, there were three battalions that constituted the brigade. We gathered near the Borike hall and set out for Obrovac. So I saw him there. He reviewed the forces there, and it seemed to me that he handed over us, so to speak, to the army Colonel Peusic or Peulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this was done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an objection. This is a subject matter that's not listed in the 65 ter summary anywhere. So I haven't had any preparations to cross-examine about this or any notification that he was going to be talking about this with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I provided my proofing note, I did give notice of this because Mr. Jankovic testified in the Stakic case and gave a statement on these issues to the Prosecutor. And I did say that he was going to be testifying to all the matters that he mentioned in his interview. Therefore, the Prosecution were on notice of what his testimony would be about. This is part of his interview. I didn't mention it specifically, but I did make reference to the interview. And there are just two issues in connection with this. He said that he saw Mr. Zupljanin twice in 1992, and I'm merely asking him to tell me about the circumstances of these two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The proofing note is four paragraphs. And it says he was shown a transcript of his interview and his testimony, and he confirmed the accuracy of his statement and the testimony regarding matters pertaining to Mr. Zupljanin. But there's no indication about being involved or handing over, something that goes to the issue of subordination, I assume. It's been a hotly contested issue in this case and certainly that something that should have required further specification than is in this proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in any event, to the extent that you -- as you plead, you haven't been prepared for this, but having regard to the length of time that you have available for cross-examination, no doubt you would be able to put yourself in the position to deal with the two issues that Mr. Krgovic has indicated he wishes to pursue. So please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But I just want to put on the record as a matter to maybe be aware of with regard to future witnesses, and the fact that this is the last matter he is bringing up with this witness suggests it's something that is very important to him because we good trial lawyers try to start with our best and finish with our best. So this was an important matter and certainly important matters are ones that deserve to be brought to the attention of the other parties in this kind of notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may respond. The last time we discussed the police brigade, Ms. Korner said that it was not an issue in dispute, that the brigade was subordinated. So I did not see that this was a matter of contention between the sides, that the police brigade was resubordinated to the army. I didn't mean to speak about resubordination at all. Rather, about him seeing Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's get on with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you please describe for us what it was that Mr. Zupljanin said when you got there and what comments, if any, your colleagues had?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to correct myself. I said that this was him handing us over. I chose the word because of the authority that he had. When I spoke to the Prosecutor, I did not choose words properly, so I said you know how it happened. Mr. Zupljanin brought along a colonel, I'm not sure what his name is. This should be double-checked. I can't recall it now even. I just said it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Peulic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Peulic. It would not have been important to me had it not happened that, in that brief introduction that Mr. Zupljanin gave of this colonel, he didn't say, I will not proceed from this place with you. I had not go with you to Orasje. Rather, it will be a colonel of our army. And then he wanted to commend him and he said, He is a senior officer who never lost a single battle. And then somebody called -- somebody among the three battalions jeered and said, And never won a single battle either. So that's why it stuck in my mind. So we didn't linger there. We boarded the buses and set off for Orasje. If that's enough for your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the second time you saw Mr. Zupljanin. And, later, in 1992, save for --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw him. He accompanied the column, but just outside of Modrica the column stopped, and Mr. Zupljanin got on our bus. I didn't even know he was going to accompany us. He asked if anybody knew which road should be taken from thereon. Everybody was silent. And then I spoke because I said that I hailed from the area. He told me, So why are you silent? Why aren't you telling me anything? And then I said, Well, I know which roads we should take, but I don't know which area was under whose control. There were Serbs and Croats there in the area. But it so happened that I went into his vehicle. He stayed behind on the bus, I believe, Zupljanin did. I went into his car, driven by a soldier, and there was this colonel in the car as well. So I directed them to take the road that I thought was best and nobody attacked us, and we reached that village of Obrovac. I never saw him again. I was there for a month and I was in the staff of the Prijedor Battalion, the commander was Simo Drljaca. I was the communications officer. I spent my time in the headquarters, and he could not possibly have visited there without me seeing him. So for that month that I was there as a communications officer in the headquarters, he never showed up. Peulic was in command of the brigade and Simo -- oh, let's me just say, briefly, that the entire organisation behind it all was military. So brigades, battalions, companies, platoons. There were some tanks attached by the army. I think two of them. And the Pragas; I think the anti-aircraft assets. Armoured vehicles and a battery of mortars. That's not the sort of weapons that the police would have by their establishment. They even had their own uniforms, those who were there with us. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. That's all I had for you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you for the extended time granted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will take the adjournment for the day. And, Mr. Jankovic, when we resume tomorrow morning, counsel on behalf of the co-accused, Stanisic, would have their questions of you, and then Mr. Hannis will begin his cross-examination. So we rise, to resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
